nameStory: The tan jumping spider gets its straightforward name from its warm, sandy-brown coloration that helps it blend perfectly with tree bark and wooden surfaces. It's also sometimes called the 'familiar jumping spider' because it's one of the most commonly encountered jumping spiders around homes and buildings, making it a familiar sight to many people.
description: The tan jumping spider is a compact, sturdy arachnid about the size of your pinky nail, typically measuring around half an inch in body length. Its fuzzy body ranges from light tan to grayish-brown, often with subtle darker markings that create a mottled appearance. Like all jumping spiders, it has a distinctly rectangular, almost box-like front section (called the cephalothorax) and remarkably large, forward-facing eyes that give it an almost curious expression. These spiders are active hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead relying on their excellent vision and impressive jumping ability.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large eyes arranged in a straight row across the front of the head, with the two center eyes noticeably larger and more prominent, like tiny black jewels that seem to track your movement

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and sturdy with a distinctly boxy front section that feels firm if gently touched, covered in short, velvety hairs that give it a slightly fuzzy texture

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Tan to grayish-brown base color with subtle darker chevron or wavy patterns on the abdomen that may be faint and require good lighting to see clearly

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length typically around 0.4-0.5 inches, with legs that don't extend dramatically beyond the body, giving it a compact rather than leggy appearance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with frequent stops to look around, often turning its entire body to face you directly when observed, and capable of impressive jumps several times its body length

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Does not build catching webs, but spins small silk retreats or draglines; look for tiny silk shelters under bark edges or in crevices where they rest

habitat: Tan jumping spiders thrive on the bark of trees, wooden fences, building exteriors, and other sun-warmed surfaces throughout New England's forests, suburbs, and urban areas. They're particularly fond of rough-textured surfaces like oak and pine bark where their coloration provides excellent camouflage. You'll often spot them on deck railings, wooden siding, and split-rail fences, especially in areas that receive partial to full sunlight during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and become active on warm, sunny days, often seen basking on sun-warmed bark and wooden surfaces. Mating displays and courtship behaviors are most common during late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most easily observed hunting during daylight hours, with females carrying egg sacs and young spiderlings dispersing. This is the best time for identification as their colors are most vibrant.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue hunting actively on warm days while preparing for winter, often found tucked into bark crevices during cooler weather. Late-season spiderlings may still be visible into early October.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter under loose bark, in wood piles, or other protected locations, becoming inactive until spring warmth returns. Occasionally seen on unusually warm winter days near heated buildings.

funFact: Tan jumping spiders have better color vision than humans, seeing well into the ultraviolet spectrum, which helps them spot the UV-reflective patterns on potential mates and prey that are completely invisible to our eyes.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small brown jumping spiders, but the tan jumping spider's relatively large size, boxy build, and distinctive straight row of four prominent front eyes set it apart. Remember: if it jumps, has huge front eyes, and looks tan like tree bark, you've likely found your spider.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'familiar,' many people don't realize they've been seeing these spiders regularly around their homes and yards, often mistaking them for other types of spiders or simply not noticing their distinctive jumping spider features.
compareHints: The tan jumping spider is the only member of its genus (Platycryptus) commonly found in New England, making identification easier than with some jumping spider groups. Compared to other regional jumping spiders, it's notably larger and more robust than the tiny zebra jumping spider, lacks the distinctive black and white stripes of that species, and has a more rectangular body shape than the rounder bold jumping spiders. Its tan coloration and preference for bark surfaces also distinguish it from the more colorful or ground-dwelling jumping spider species in the region.
